Surah al-Qamar (The Moon)

Meccan, except verses 44, 45 and 46, which are Medinan. Its verses number fifty-five.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has been split.﴾ It is related that the disbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a sign, and the moon was split. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: It split into two halves, one half departed and one half remained. Ibn Mas'ud said: "I saw Hira' between the two halves of the moon." And from 'Uthman ibn 'Ata', from his father, that its meaning is: it will split on the Day of Resurrection. This is refuted by His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 2:

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ Its meaning indicates that it has occurred, and that they have witnessed it after witnessing its like. It is also read as "وقَدِ انْشَقَّ القَمَرُ" (wa-qad inshaqqa al-qamar, "and the moon has split"), meaning: the Hour has drawn near, and among the signs of its approach has occurred the splitting of the moon. The meaning of "الِاسْتِمْرارِ" (al-istimrar, continuity) is either "الِاطِّرادُ" (al-ittirad, regularity) or "الِاسْتِحْكامُ" (al-istihkam, firmness), that is: and if they see a sign from the signs of Allah, they turn away from reflecting upon it, so that they would not stop to recognize its truth and its exalted rank, and they say: "sihrun mutta'arid da'im" (a regular, lasting magic) which Muhammad brings across the passage of time, never really varying in any state, like all kinds of magic; or "qawiyyun mustahkim" (a strong, firmly established magic) that cannot be removed. It has also been said: "mustamirr" means passing and going away, not remaining, as a wishful consolation to themselves; and as a rationale, which is the most fitting, by their extremism in obstinacy and arrogance; and what will come later in refutation of it supports this. It is also read as "وَإنْ يُرَوْا" (wa-in yuraw), in the passive voice from the verb "al-ira'a" (to show).

"And they denied": that is, they denied the Prophet ﷺ and what they witnessed of the miracles that Allah the Exalted displayed at his hand.

"And followed their desires": which Satan had made attractive to them. Or, they denied the sign, which is the splitting of the moon, and followed their desires, and they said: "The moon has been bewitched," or "Our eyes have been bewitched, while the moon remains in its state." The past tense is used to indicate certainty.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "And every matter is settled" (﴿وَكُلُّ أمْرٍ مُسْتَقِرٌّ﴾), it is a resumptive sentence, brought to despair them of what they had hung their empty hopes upon, namely that his affair ﷺ would not be settled, as they had said: "It is continuous magic." It shows its permanence and firmness; that is, every matter among matters is settled, that is, it ends at a limit upon which it will inevitably come to rest. Among these matters is the affair of the Prophet ﷺ, which will reach a limit at which its truth and the loftiness of his standing will become clear. The vagueness regarding that upon which it is settled serves to draw attention to the perfect manifestness of the situation and to the lack of need to state it explicitly.

It has also been said: the meaning is that every matter of theirs and of his ﷺ is settled, that is, it will be established and settle into a state of abandonment or victory in this world, and misery or happiness in the Hereafter.

It was also read with a fatha (mustaqarr), as a verbal noun, or as a noun of place, or as a noun of time, meaning: possessing settledness, or possessing a place of settledness, or possessing a time of settledness. And it was read with a kasra and a genitive case (mustaqarrin), as an attribute of "amr," and "kull" is conjoined to "as-sa'ah," meaning: the Hour has drawn near, and every settled matter [has drawn near].

And indeed there has come to them ﴿from the news﴾, i.e., in the Qur'an, and His saying ﴿from the news﴾, i.e., the news of the past generations or the news of the Hereafter, is related to something omitted that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) modifying what follows, i.e., "And by Allah, indeed there has come to them [news] being from the news."

﴿In which there is a deterrent﴾, i.e., a restraint from punishment or threat; or it is a place of restraint, on the basis that "fī" is taǧrīdiyya (the particle "fī" is used to denote that the thing itself is the container, as a figurative abstraction), and the meaning is that it is in itself a place of restraint. The tā' of the iftiʿāl form (ittiʿāl-form, the reflexive verbal pattern) is changed to dāl before dāl, dhāl, and zāy for the sake of harmony, and it was read as "muzzajar" with the tā' changed to zāy and assimilated.

**﴿Far-reaching wisdom﴾**, whose ultimate end is free of any defect. It is either a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for "*ma*" or the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject. It is also read in the accusative (*manṣūb*) as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of it, since "*ma*" is either a relative (*mawṣūlah*) or a qualified noun (*mawṣūfah*) that has been specified by its attribute, so the accusative of the circumstantial qualifier is permissible from it.

**﴿So warnings avail not﴾**: this is a negation of benefit, or a denial of it. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of the absence of benefit upon the coming of far-reaching wisdom, although warnings were expected to benefit. The present-tense form indicates the renewal of the absence of benefit and its continuance, according to the renewal and continuance of the arrival of admonitions. "*Ma*" on the second view is in the accusative, meaning: "what benefit, then, do warnings bring?" *Nudhur* is the plural of *nadhīr* in the sense of "the warner," or a verbal noun meaning "warning."

**﴿So turn away from them﴾**, because of your knowledge that warning will have no effect on them whatsoever.

**﴿The day the Caller calls﴾**: this is in the accusative case, governed either by "they will come forth" (yakhrujūn) or by "remember" (udhkur). The caller is Israfil (ʿalayhi al-salām). It is permissible for the calling here to be like the command in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be, and it is﴾, and the dropping of the yāʾ (of "dāʿī") is for sufficiency with the kasra, as a lightening.

**﴿To a thing terrible﴾**: i.e., a dreadful, terrible matter that souls find strange, since they have no precedent for its like, and it is the terror of the Resurrection. It has also been read as "nukr" with the sukun (lightened), and "nukira," meaning "unknown/unrecognized" (uncommon in the sense of unfamiliar, i.e., "unknown" in the sense of "unrecognized").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 7:

﴿Humbled their eyes﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of ﴿they will come forth﴾, and it is placed first because the governing verb is flexible (mutaṣarrif), meaning: they will come forth ﴿from the graves﴾ humbled, their eyes lowered from the intensity of the terror. It is also read "khāshi'an" (humbled, singular and masculine), and the singular and masculine form is used because its subject is an apparent noun that is not truly feminine. It is also read "khāshi'ah" (feminine) according to the original form, and it is read "khushsha'un abṣāruhum" (their eyes are humbled), in the form of a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), so that the clause is a circumstantial clause.

﴿As if they were scattered locusts﴾ in their multitude, their surging, and their dispersal in all directions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 8:

﴿Hastening towards the Summoner﴾: rushing, stretching out their necks towards him, or gazing at him.

﴿The disbelievers will say﴾: this is a resumed statement (isti'naf), which comes as an answer to what arises from the description of the Day, its terrors, and the state of its people in their dire condition, as if it were said: "What will happen then?" So it is said: the disbelievers will say, ﴿This is a difficult day﴾, meaning: hard and severe. In attributing the mentioned saying to the disbelievers there is an allusion that the believers are not at that degree of severity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 9:

﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ This begins an enumeration of some of the reports mentioned that are conducive to admonition, and a kind of detailed explanation of them, and a statement of their lack of response to them, as confirmation of the import of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So of what avail were the warnings?﴾ That is: the people of Noah committed denial before the denial of your people. His words, exalted is He, ﴿so they denied Our servant﴾ are an explanation of that vague denial, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Noah called upon his Lord and said, "My Lord..."﴾ etc. In it there is further confirmation and affirmation of the denial. It has also been said: its meaning is: they denied him with denial following denial, whenever a denying generation passed away from among them, another denying generation like it came after it. It has also been said: the people of Noah denied the messengers, so they denied Our servant, because he was one of them. And in mentioning him, peace be upon him, with the title of servitude together with the attribution to the plural of majesty (the "Nun" of greatness), is an exaltation of him, peace be upon him, a raising of his station, and an increase in reproach of his deniers.

﴿And they said, "Possessed"﴾ That is: they did not restrict themselves to mere denial, but ascribed to him madness.

﴿And he was rebuffed﴾ This is coordinated with "they said": that is, he was restrained from conveying the message by various kinds of harm. It has also been said: it is part of what they said, that is: he is possessed, and the jinn have rebuffed him and driven him mad.

**﴿So he called upon his Lord: "That﴾** — i.e., "that"; it is also read with a kasra (*innī*), on the understanding that it is a verb of saying (*irādat al-qawl*).

**﴿I am overcome﴾** — i.e., by my people; I have no power to take revenge upon them.

**﴿So help [me]﴾** — i.e., take revenge for me upon them. This comes after his despair of them having been firmly established, following "the many years and the years" (*al-latayā wa'l-latī*) of his preaching. It is related that when one of them met him, he would throttle him until he fell down unconscious, and [Nuh] would say: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know."

"So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down," pouring forth in torrents. This is a depiction of the abundance of the rains and the intensity of their pouring; and it was read "fa-fattahna" with the doubled letter (tashdid), indicating the multiplicity of the gates.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 12:

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾. That is: We made the whole earth as though it were gushing springs. The original wording was "and We caused the springs of the earth to burst forth," but it was changed for the sake of the requirements of the context (qada'an li-haqqi al-maqam).

﴿So the waters met﴾. That is: the water of the sky and the water of the earth. The singular form (al-ma') is used to affirm that the meeting of the two waters was not merely by way of adjacency and proximity, but by way of mixing and becoming one. It is also read as "al-ma'an" (the two waters), because of the difference between the two kinds, and as "al-ma'wan," with the hamza changed to a waw.

﴿for a matter already decreed﴾. That is: existing in a state which Allah Most High had already determined, without any disparity; or, in a state that was measured and made equal, namely that what was sent down was measured according to what was brought forth. Or, it means a matter which Allah Most High had decreed, namely the destruction of the people of Noah by the flood.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 13:**

﴿And We bore him﴾, that is, Noah, peace be upon him.

﴿Upon a [vessel] of planks and nails﴾, that is, of broad pieces of wood.

﴿And nails﴾, meaning nails (masamir), the plural of disar, from al-dasr, which is "propulsion" (al-daf'). It is an attribute of the ship, and it stands in its place in that it serves as an explanation of it, performing its function.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 14:

﴿Sailing⁠ under our eyes⁠﴾ in our sight, i.e., preserved by our protection. (p-170) ﴿As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved⁠﴾, i.e., We did that as a recompense to Nuh, upon him be peace, because he was a blessing that they disbelieved in. For every prophet is a blessing from Allah the Exalted upon his community and a mercy, and what a blessing and what a mercy! It has also been permitted that it be (read as) "for one who was disbelieved," by omitting the preposition and connecting the verb to the pronoun, and its concealment within the verb after it has been changed to the nominative. And it has been recited as "for one who disbelieved (لِمَن كَفَرَ)," i.e., for the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 15:

﴿And We left it as a sign﴾. That is: the ship, or the deed (al-fi'lah).

﴿A sign﴾ by which whoever comes to know its account takes heed. Qatadah said: Allah, exalted is He, preserved it in the land of al-Jazirah. It was also said: upon al-Judi for a long age, until the earliest of this community looked upon it.

﴿Then is there any who will take heed?﴾ That is: one who takes admonition from that sign, which truly merits being heeded. It was recited as "muddakir" (mudhtakir) in its original form, and as "muddakir" with the ta' converted into dhal and assimilated into it (idgham).

Translation:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 16:

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ This is an interrogative of magnification and wonder, meaning: they were of a dreadful nature that description cannot encompass. And "nudhur" (warnings) is the plural of "nadhir" (warner), in the sense of "indhar" (warning).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 17:

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ ... etc. This is an oath-clause, which occurs at the end of the four stories, confirming the content of what preceded it in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And there had certainly come to them of the news that which contained a deterrent, far-reaching wisdom; but warning benefits not﴾, and as an indication that each story among them is independently sufficient to necessitate remembrance and to suffice for restraint, and yet not one of them has been taken into consideration. That is: "And by Allah, We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for your people, by sending it down in their language, and by filling it with kinds of admonitions and lessons, and by varying in it the threats and promises."

﴿For remembrance﴾, that is: for taking heed and being admonished.

﴿So is there any who will take heed?﴾ This is a denial and negation of one who is admonished, in the most emphatic and forceful manner, since it indicates that no one can answer the questioner with "yes." Carrying its facilitation to mean making its memorization easy, by the eloquence of its composition and the sweetness of its words and expressions, does not fit the context.

"Ad denied (the messenger)." That is, Hud, peace be upon him. He does not mention the manner of their denial, for the sake of brevity and in haste to state what contains warning of the punishment. His words, exalted is He, "So how was My punishment and warnings?" are to direct the hearts of the listeners to attentively listen to what is conveyed to them before it is mentioned, not to magnify or exalt it, nor to make them marvel at its state after its explanation, as is the case with what precedes it and what follows it. It is as if it were said: "Ad denied, so have you heard, or listen: how was My punishment and My warnings to them?"

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 19:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what was stated in summary earlier. That is: We sent upon them a wind that was cold, or one that was loud and violent in its sound.

﴿On a day of ill omen﴾: of misfortune (shu'm).

﴿Continuous﴾: that is, its misfortune persisted, or it remained upon them until it destroyed them, or it encompassed all of them, great and small, or its bitterness was intense. And it was a Wednesday at the end of the month.

(p-171) ﴿تَنْزِعُ النّاسَ﴾ "tanzi'u al-nas" means it uproots them (taqla'uhum). It is related that they entered the ravines and the pits, and some of them clung to others, but the wind pulled them out and threw them down dead.

﴿كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾ That is, uprooted from its place of planting. It was said: they were likened to "a'jaz al-nakhl" (the trunks of palm trees), which are its roots without branches, because the wind would uproot their heads, leaving bodies and trunks without heads. The masculine form of the attribute of the palm (munqa'ir) is used in view of the word (lafz), just as its feminine form in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a'jazu nakhlin khawiyah﴾ ("trunks of hollow palm trees") is used in view of the meaning (ma'na).

Allah's saying: ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ is a means of expressing the awfulness of what befell them (tahwil) and of marveling at their condition (ta'jib) after it has been made clear. Therefore there is no trace of repetition in it. As for what has been said, that the first refers to what befell them in this world and the second to what will befall them in the Hereafter, this is refuted by the fact that the second is ordered upon the worldly punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 22:

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance; so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ The discussion regarding it is like that which passed earlier in what preceded.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 23:

﴿Thamud denied the warnings.﴾ That is: the admonitions and exhortations they heard from Salih, or [the warnings brought] by the messengers, peace be upon them. For the denial of any one of them is a denial of all of them, since they agree on the fundamentals of the sacred laws (shara'i').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 24:

﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among ourselves?"﴾ That is, one who is of our kind. Its accusative status (intisab, i.e., its grammatical case as an object) is due to a verb that is explained by what follows it.

﴿A single one﴾: that is, one who stands alone without followers, or one individual from among their ordinary members and not from among their nobles. It is another attribute of "a human being" (basharan). Its being placed after the attribute that was interpreted (the clause "from among ourselves") serves as an alert that both being of our kind (al-jinsiyyah) and being single (al-wahdah) are each something that prevents following. Had it been placed before that attribute, this subtle point would have been lost. It is also read as "Abashrun minna wahidun" (Is a human being from among us, a single one...?), in the nominative as an inceptive (mubtada'), with His statement ﴿we follow him﴾ as its predicate (khabar). The first reading is more eloquent because of the interrogative sense.

﴿Then indeed we would be﴾: that is, on the supposition that we follow him while he stands alone and we are a vast community.

﴿Surely in error﴾: away from what is right.

﴿And madness﴾: that is, insanity, for that is far removed from the demands of reason. It has also been said: he used to tell them, "If you do not follow me, you are in error from the truth and in fire (su'ur)," su'ur being the plural of sa'ir (blazing fire). Out of extreme obstinacy they reversed this against him, peace be upon him, saying: "If we follow you, then we would indeed be as you say."

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ That is: the Book and the Revelation.

﴿Upon him from among us?﴾ Meaning: there are among us those who are more worthy of it than he is.

﴿Nay, he is a liar, an insolent one.﴾ That is: the matter is not as they say; rather, he is such-and-such. His arrogance (baṭar) led him to set himself above us through what he claimed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 26:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent one﴾. It is a narration of what He, exalted is He, said to Salih, peace be upon him, as a promise to him and a threat to his people. The sin (sin) here is for bringing the content of the sentence closer and emphasizing it. By "tomorrow" is meant the time of the descent of the punishment, i.e., they will surely know soon who is the liar, the insolent one whose arrogance and haughtiness led him to self-exaltation: is Salih the one, or is it the one who denied him? It is read as "sa-ta'lamun" (you will know) by way of iltifat (shift of address), to intensify the rebuke, or as a narration of what Salih answered them with. It is read as "al-ashir" like their saying "hadhir fi hadhar" (wary, in extreme wariness). It is read as "al-ashharr," i.e., the most emphatic in wickedness, and this is a rejected form, like "al-akhir." It was said: by "tomorrow" is meant the Day of Resurrection, but his saying, exalted is He, refutes this:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾ ... etc. It is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain the beginnings of what was promised as certain, that is: We will bring her out from the rocky height (hadabah) just as they asked.

﴿As a trial for them﴾ means: as a test (imtihan).

﴿So watch them﴾ means: so wait for them and observe (tabassur) what they do.

﴿And be patient﴾ over their harm (adhiyyah).

[Verse 28] "And inform them that the water is to be shared between them," each allotted a day for herself and a day for them. "Between them" is in the masculine plural to give precedence to rational beings (lit. "for the prevailing of the rational ones").

"Every drink is to be attended," that is, each party attends the water on its own turn.

﴿So they called to their companion, and he took (the sword) and hamstrung (the she-camel).﴾ The companion is Qudar ibn Salif, the wretched one of Thamud (Ahaymir Thamud).

﴿So he took (it) and hamstrung (her).﴾ He dared to undertake the great deed, paying it no heed, and so he committed the hamstringing of the she-camel. It is also said: "he took hold of the she-camel and hamstrung her," or "he took up the sword and slew her." Ta'ati (taʿāṭī) means taking hold of a thing with effort.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 30:

﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ The discussion here is like that which passed at the beginning of the story of 'Ad.

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single shout﴾. It was the shout of Gabriel, peace be upon him.

﴿So they became﴾, i.e., they became.

﴿Like the crumbled remains of one who makes a hazira﴾, i.e., like the dry wood that the one who builds the enclosure (hazira) gathers for building it, or like the dry grass that the owner of the enclosure gathers for his livestock in winter. It was also read with a fatha on the ẓā', i.e., ﴿like the crumbled remains of the hazira﴾, or of the tree taken for it (al-muttakhadh li-ha).

Note on the recitation: the word here is ﴿المُحْتَظِرِ﴾ (al-muḥtaẓir) with a kasra on the ẓā', meaning the one who makes the enclosure. The variant reading with a fatha, ﴿الحَظِيرَةِ﴾ (al-ḥaẓīrah), makes the word refer to the enclosure itself rather than the person who builds it.

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single shout﴾. It was the shout of Gabriel, peace be upon him.

﴿So they became﴾, i.e., they became.

﴿Like the crumbled remains of one who makes a hazira﴾, i.e., like the dry wood that the one who builds the enclosure (hazira) gathers for building it, or like the dry grass that the owner of the enclosure gathers for his livestock in winter. It was also read with a fatha on the ẓā', i.e., ﴿like the crumbled remains of the hazira﴾, or of the tree taken for it (al-muttakhadh li-ha).

Note on the recitation: the word here is ﴿المُحْتَظِرِ﴾ (al-muḥtaẓir) with a kasra on the ẓā', meaning the one who makes the enclosure. The variant reading with a fatha, ﴿الحَظِيرَةِ﴾ (al-ḥaẓīrah), makes the word refer to the enclosure itself rather than the person who builds it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verses 33–34:

﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings﴾, ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind (ḥāṣib)﴾, i.e., a wind that pelts them (taḥṣibuhum), i.e., strikes them with pebbles (al-ḥaṣbāʾ).

﴿Except the family of Lot; We saved them at dawn (bi-saḥar)﴾: "at a time of dawn (saḥar)," which is the last part of the night. It is also said that it is the last sixth of the night, i.e., they were in the state of being at dawn (bi-saḥar).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verses 33–34:

﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings﴾, ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind (ḥāṣib)﴾, i.e., a wind that pelts them (taḥṣibuhum), i.e., strikes them with pebbles (al-ḥaṣbāʾ).

﴿Except the family of Lot; We saved them at dawn (bi-saḥar)﴾: "at a time of dawn (saḥar)," which is the last part of the night. It is also said that it is the last sixth of the night, i.e., they were in the state of being at dawn (bi-saḥar).

"Grace from Us" (ni'mah min 'indina): that is, a favour from Us; and it is the reason (ʿillah) for "We delivered" (najjaynā).

"Thus" (kadhālika): that is, like that wondrous recompense.

"We reward those who are thankful" (najzī man shakara): for Our blessing, by faith and obedience.

And indeed Lot had warned them (﴿وَلَقَدْ أنْذَرَهُمْ﴾), (peace be upon him).

﴿بَطْشَتَنا﴾: that is, Our severe seizure with punishment.

﴿فَتَمارَوْا﴾: then they denied (فَكَذَّبُوا).

﴿بِالنُّذُرِ﴾: while doubting (مُتَشاكِّينَ).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 37:**

﴿And they had sought to seduce him from his guests﴾: they intended lewdness with them.

﴿So We obliterated their eyes﴾: We wiped them smooth and leveled them like the rest of the face. It is related that when they entered his house by force, Jibril (peace be upon him) struck them with a single blow, and he left them groping, unable to find the door, until Lut (peace be upon him) brought them out.

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings﴾: that is, We said to them, through the tongues of the angels, "Taste," or the apparent state of affairs. What is meant by it is the obliteration, for it is among the punishments they were warned of.

Translation:

﴿And indeed, an early morning assault came upon them at dawn﴾. It is also read "bukratan" (without tanwin, i.e., ghayr munsarifa), on the basis that what is meant by it is the beginning of the day, specified (as such).

﴿A lasting punishment﴾: one that does not leave them until they are delivered to the Fire. And in describing it as "lasting" (mustaqirr) there is a hint that the punishment of obliteration (al-tams) that came before it ends in this one.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 39:

﴿So taste My punishment and My warnings.﴾ This is a recounting of what is said at that time from His part, exalted is He, as an intensification of the punishment.
﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ What was said in it has already passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 41:

﴿And indeed there came to the family of Pharaoh the warnings.﴾ Their story is introduced with an oath-based emphasis (al-tawkid al-qasami) to display the utmost care given to its matter, owing to the greatness of the signs it contains and their abundance, the terror of the punishment they encountered, and the strength of its call to admonition. The mention of "the family of Pharaoh" alone is sufficient, since it is known that Pharaoh himself is more deserving of this (warning). That is: "By Allah, indeed there came to them the warnings."

Almighty God's saying: ﴿They denied Our signs﴾ is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf), built upon a question that arose from the narration of the coming of the warners, as if it were said: "What did they do then?" So it is said: they denied all Our signs, and these are the nine signs.

﴿Then We seized them with the seizure of One Mighty﴾ who cannot be overcome.

﴿Omnipotent﴾ nothing can frustrate Him.

﴿Are your disbelievers﴾ O assembly of the Arabs,

﴿better﴾ in strength, might, equipment and numbers, or in standing, than ﴿those﴾, the disbelievers previously mentioned? The meaning is: they were struck by what struck them even though their superiority over you in the matters mentioned was evident. So do you hope that the like of that will not befall you, when you are worse than them in standing and in a worse condition? And His saying, ﴿Or do you have immunity in the scriptures﴾, is a turning away and a shift from rebuke to another mode. That is: rather, do you have immunity and security from the consequences of what you do of disbelief and sins, and their calamities, written in the heavenly books, so that you persist in what you are upon?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 44:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united body that will be victorious"?﴾ is a transition (idrab) of rebuke (tabkit), and the shift from direct address to third person (al-iltifat) serves to signal that their state calls for turning away from them and removing them from the rank of being addressed directly, and for relating their ugly deeds to others. That is: "Rather, do they say, confident in their power, 'We are people of resolve and opinion, our affair is unified, we cannot be overpowered nor humiliated'? Or 'victorious over the enemies, we will not be defeated'? Or 'mutually supporting, each of us helps the other'?" The singular form (al-ifrad) is used in view of the wording of jami' (the collective).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 45:

Allah's saying: ﴿Soon will the multitude be defeated﴾ is a rejection and refutation of that (claim), and the sin (in sa-) is for emphasis, meaning: their multitude will certainly be defeated.

﴿And they will turn their backs﴾, that is, "their backs" (al-adbar). It has also been read thus, and the singular (dubur) is for the sense of the category (iradat al-jins), or for the sense that each one of them will turn his back. This was indeed the case on the day of Badr. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) say: "When there was revealed ﴿Soon will the multitude be defeated and they will turn their backs﴾, I did not know which multitude would be defeated. Then, on the day of Badr, I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wearing his armour and saying: ﴿Soon will the multitude be defeated and they will turn their backs﴾, and then I understood its interpretation."

It was also read as "sa-yahzimu al-jam'a" (with the verb active), meaning: Allah, Mighty and Exalted, will defeat the multitude.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 46:

﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time⁠﴾ That is: this is not the completion of their punishment; rather, the Hour is the appointed time for the root of their torment, and this (worldly suffering) is among its precursors.

﴿And the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter⁠﴾ That is: it is at the utmost extreme of horror, bitterness and calamity (dahya). "Dahya" (a severe, overwhelming calamity) is the dreadful matter from which no escape can be found. The mention of "the Hour" in the place where a pronoun would be expected serves to heighten its terrifying nature.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 47:**

﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾ (are) among the first and the last.

﴿are in error and madness﴾. That is: in destruction and in fires kindled (musa''ara). It was also said: in error from the truth in the world, and in fires in the Hereafter.

"And His saying: ﴿On the day they are dragged﴾ ...etc. is in the accusative case, either governed by what is understood from His saying ﴿in error﴾, meaning: they are in error and blazing fire on the day they are dragged,

﴿into the Fire on their faces﴾. Or it is governed by a verb of saying implied after it, meaning: on the day they are dragged, it will be said to them: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar﴾, meaning: experience its heat and its pain. Saqar is a name of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined, from saqarathu al-nar (the fire scorched him) and saqarathu when it blackens him. The implied saying, according to the first way, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they are dragged"."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 49:

﴿Indeed, We have created everything﴾ of things.

﴿in measure﴾ That is: bound up with a specific measure that the wisdom upon which the affair of creation (al-takwin) turns has required, or determined and written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh) before its occurrence. "Kulla shay'" (everything) is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by what follows it (a construction known as ishtighal, "occupation"), and it has been read in the nominative, in which case it is the subject (mubtada') and "khalaqnahu" (We have created it) is its predicate (khabar).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 50:

﴿And Our command is but one [word], like a glance of the eye.﴾ That is: one word, swift in coming into being, which is His saying, exalted is He, "Be" (kun); or, "but one act," which is the bringing into existence without any effort or treatment.

﴿Like a glance of the eye﴾ in ease and speed. It has also been said that its meaning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the command of the Hour is but like a glance of the eye﴾.

"And We had already destroyed your like" (ashyā'akum): that is, your counterparts in disbelief among the nations. It was also said: your followers.

"So is there anyone who will take heed?" who will be admonished by that.

And every thing they have done, of disbelief and acts of disobedience, is written down in detail. (﴿وَكُلُّ شَيْءٍ فَعَلُوهُ﴾: "And everything they have done.")

﴿فِي الزُّبُرِ﴾ means: in the registers of the recording angels (ḥafaẓa, the guardian angels who record deeds).

﴿And every small and great [deed]﴾ of the deeds.

﴿Is recorded﴾: written down in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the heavenly record) in its full details. Since the description of the disbelievers' bad state, in His words, ﴿Indeed the criminals﴾, calls for a description of the good state of the believers, so that warning and encouragement are balanced, [the author] mentions what they have of good state in summary. So it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 54:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ i.e., those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins.

﴿will be in gardens﴾ of great stature.

﴿and a river﴾ i.e., rivers likewise. The singular is used because the generic noun suffices, with consideration for the rhyme (fawasil, the closing rhymed endings of verses). It is also read as "nuhr" (nuhr), the plural of nahar (nahar), like usd (usd) and asad (asad).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 54, verse 55:

﴿In a seat of truth﴾ in a pleasing place. It is also read "in seats of truth" (fi maqa'id sidq).

﴿in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ i.e., drawn near in the presence of a King whose dominion and authority cannot be measured, so that nothing exists except that it is under His dominion (malakut). Exalted is He; how great is His station!

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Qamar every ghibb (every other day, or at intervals), Allah will raise him on the Day of Resurrection with a face like the full moon on the night of the full moon."
